Thanks for the time earlier — great discussion. Quick recap + agreed follow-ups: 

Summary of requirements we captured on the call:
- Target latency: p95 <= 150ms for short generation requests (<256 tokens); soft p99 objective <= 300ms for interactive flows.
- Peak concurrency: ~1,200 concurrent active requests during peak in-region traffic.
- Throughput profile: steady background embedding workload + spiky generation bursts; expected 10k tokens/sec sustained during business hours with bursts up to 40k tokens/sec for short windows.
- Streaming: customers require real-time token streaming for chat product (SSE/websocket support).
- SLO: 99.9% availability, and latency SLOs above. Queueing above 1s impacts user experience.

Open questions we promised to answer:
1) Scale-up time from idle to required capacity for burst traffic (including warm pool behavior).
2) How warm pools and pre-warmed model instances affect p95/p99 latency.
3) Expected queuing behavior under sustained overload and recommended queue thresholds.
4) Cost tradeoffs for keeping warm pools vs cold starts.

Attachments: I’ve attached the SLO matrix + a short design doc (redwood-autoscale-design.pdf) with notes from the call.

Next steps / asks:
- Rishi: can you provide a short note on autoscaling behavior (scale-up windows, warm pool sizing heuristics, and queueing policy) we can share with the Eng team at Acme?
- Aditya: I’ll schedule a follow-up demo/POC for next week; please come with a rough SLA/commitment for Dedicated capacity options.

Hey team — digging into the numbers and behavior based on our runtime + Dedicated options. High-level summary first, then a short table with ballpark numbers.

Key behavior notes:
- Cold start (0 warm instances): starting a model instance (load model weights, init kernels) typically takes ~45–120s depending on model size and quantization. For our largest curated models this trends toward the upper end. Cold starts are the main contributor to slow scale-ups.
- Warm pools: keeping a pre-initialized instance (warm) reduces scale-up to ~2–6s to start serving (socket ready + auth + KV cache warmup for small contexts). Warm pool hits are essentially warm-starts and produce near steady-state latency.
- Steady-state scaling (autoscale up by adding warmed replicas from a warm pool) can reach target concurrency faster when warm pool size is adequate; in practice, adding an already-warm replica contributes capacity in ~2–10s.
- Burst handling vs queueing: our routing has a short in-memory queue with configurable thresholds. If concurrency hits the configured limit: 
  - Option A (queue): requests are queued up to X ms (customer-configurable); queued requests still consume memory but avoid immediate rejections. Long queueing increases client-side latency and can violate SLOs.
  - Option B (reject/fallback): return a fast 5xx or fallback content; better UX in some streaming cases (allows client-side fallback to cached response).
- Streaming: our streaming path (SSE/ws) is supported end-to-end. Streaming helps perceived latency, but SLOs measured on token-level completion still apply.

Ballpark table (for short generation flows, <256 tokens) — p95 / p99 / scale-up time:
- Cold (no warm pool): p95 ~ 700–1200ms, p99 ~ 1500–2500ms, scale-up 45–120s (node init depend).
- Warm pool (1 warm instance per model replica): p95 ~ 140–180ms, p99 ~ 300–450ms, scale-up 2–10s (depending on orchestration + socket warmup).
- Steady-state (already scaled): p95 ~ 110–150ms, p99 ~ 200–350ms, immediate (0–2s) to accept new requests if capacity available.

Sizing heuristics / recommendations:
1) Warm pool sizing: for spiky user-driven traffic with spikes in 30–60s, recommend keeping warm instances equal to ~10–20% of sustained peak concurrency. For ACME’s peak ~1,200 concurrent, that’s ~120–240 warm replicas (regionally distributed).
2) Warm pool cost: warm instances bill at a reduced warm rate (we can provide precise $/hr in SLA doc); cost vs SLO: 10% warm gives large p95 improvements with moderate cost; 50% warm reduces p99 but scales cost linearly.
3) Autoscale policy: use aggressive scale-up threshold (start provisioning when queue > 10% of concurrency) with short primary queueing window (<=500ms) to avoid SLO violation. Use graceful degradation/fallback when queue > 1s.
4) Cache/KV suggestions: prefix caching and KV reuse reduce cold-start token work; preloading common prompts can shave ~20–50ms on steady-state p95 for chat flows.

Notes on measurement: we should align on p95 window (rolling 5m vs 1h) and synthetic load tests to validate. For procurement SLOs, recommend stating p95 targets as 5m rolling with an exception policy for node provisioning events.

Happy to convert this to a short table for Sofia/Carlos and include an illustrative cost delta for 10/25/50% warm pools.

— Rishi
Principal Solutions Architect | Redwood Inference

Sofia — thanks for the follow-ups and great questions.

Summary of what Rishi provided (short version for procurement):
- Cold-start scale-up is non-trivial (45–120s) and will increase p95/p99 during that window.
- Warm pools reduce scale-up to ~2–10s and bring p95 into target range; recommended warm pool sizing: 10–20% of peak concurrency (~120–240 warm replicas for your estimated peak).
- Queueing: we recommend a short configurable queue (<=500ms) for smoothing micro-bursts; beyond ~1s prefer fallback/reject to avoid UX abandonment.

Action items / next steps:
1) Technical POC: Rishi and Aditya will run a short POC next week to validate p95/p99 at 10% and 25% warm pool sizes (estimated runtime: 2 days).
2) Cost estimate: Aditya will provide a warm-pool cost delta for 10/25/50% options plus a proposed Dedicated SLA for 99.9% availability.
3) Procurement language: I’ll draft suggested SLA wording that references rolling p95 (5m) and an exception clause for provisioning events; will circulate for review.

Can you confirm Mon/Tue availability for the POC (I proposed Mon 07/06 at 10am PT)? If that works I’ll send calendar invites and include the POC test plan.
